title: Studies in Modern Movement

jokes.text: Some dude peed on my car while I was parking it. Oh, you met Spaghetti.
jokes.setup: Someone complains a dude peed on their car while parking — a gross, alarming event
jokes.punchline: Annie casually identifies the culprit by nickname ('Spaghetti'), normalizing it as a known neighborhood fixture
jokes.explanation: The punchline works on two levels: it confirms the neighborhood is genuinely terrible AND reveals Annie is so accustomed to it she's on a first-name basis with the local urinator. The nickname 'Spaghetti' is perfectly absurd. Economical and character-revealing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm glad you're getting out of that neighborhood, Annie.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, last week someone urinated on my car while I was actively parking.

jokes.text: Speaking of missing people, how did Jeff dodge this bullet... of friendship.
jokes.setup: Britta starts a sentence that sounds like she's going to call moving a burden or chore
jokes.punchline: She catches herself and tacks on 'of friendship' with unconvincing enthusiasm, exposing the group's forced positivity
jokes.explanation: Classic Community group-dynamic joke — the half-hearted correction betrays everyone's true feelings. Works efficiently but isn't particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh, you mean Spaghetti? Yeah, he pees on cars.

jokes.text: There'll be a honeymoon phase, but it won't be long till you hate their guts.
jokes.setup: Annie is enthusiastically excited about moving in with Troy and Abed
jokes.punchline: Shirley flatly predicts she will come to hate them, with the casual certainty of someone who has lived this
jokes.explanation: Functional but familiar sitcom wisdom delivered as a buzzkill. The humor comes from Shirley's blunt certainty, which is character-consistent, but the observation itself isn't particularly fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I dodged a bullet.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: How did you dodge an actual bullet?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, I mean I dodged a bullet metaphorically.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Oh, friendship.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, I forgot. You're 20. Don't worry. It's natural.
jokes.setup: Annie says she'll never hate Troy and Abed; Shirley treats this as adorable naivety
jokes.punchline: Shirley patronizes her by attributing the delusion to youth — 'You're 20. Don't worry. It's natural.' — as if optimism is a developmental phase you grow out of
jokes.explanation: Shirley's condescension is perfectly calibrated — she's not being cruel, just insufferably wise. The 'Don't worry, it's natural' reframe of idealism as a curable adolescent condition is sharp and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh, shut your mouth!

jokes.text: When you become roommates with friends, the things you love become the things that make you wanna smother them. But that's unacceptable to me. / Then I'm lying?
jokes.setup: Shirley makes a talking-head prediction that living with friends leads to wanting to smother them, then adds 'But that's unacceptable to me'
jokes.punchline: Cut to: 'Then I'm lying?' — implying Shirley is literally threatening to smother someone off-camera or is being pushed back on, making her moral caveat immediately absurd
jokes.explanation: Classic mockumentary cut joke — the talking head plants a caveat, then the next beat undercuts it. The 'Then I'm lying?' implies Shirley's restraint is already failing. Good structural use of the format.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I just don't think I could ever hate any of you guys. I mean, we're roommates. We're basically family.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's because you're young. Wait until you've lived with someone for a few years. You'll hate them. You'll hate them so much.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I don't think that will happen with us.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh, sweetie. Give it time.

jokes.text: We're here to help you move on the dance floor. / We're live-tweeting Annie's Move. Hashtag: Annie's Move.
jokes.setup: Everyone is helping Annie move; Troy and Abed show up seemingly to help
jokes.punchline: They reframe 'move' as dancing and announce they're live-tweeting the move instead of physically helping
jokes.explanation: Very Troy-and-Abed — they've gamified and spectacularized a mundane task while contributing nothing practical. The wordplay on 'move' is light but the character specificity makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's completely unacceptable.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, is it though?

jokes.text: How was I supposed to know it was a handicap space? The man in the wheelchair was yelling it. Oh, yeah, and he doesn't have an agenda.
jokes.setup: Britta apparently parked in a handicap space; someone points out the person in a wheelchair was yelling at her
jokes.punchline: Britta dismisses the wheelchair user's complaint as an 'agenda' — a satirical jab at Britta's brand of weaponized progressive skepticism backfiring
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. It perfectly skewers Britta's character flaw — her progressive pretensions curdled into reflexive contrarianism. Accusing a wheelchair user of having an 'agenda' for yelling at her about a handicap space is an inspired satirical inversion. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're here to help you move these boxes.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, we got you.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Ready? And five, six, seven, eight!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Wait, what are we—

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're dancing!

jokes.text: So you're sick, huh? Uh, that's what they tell me. Cut the wit, Winger. Where are you, the Gap or Banana Republic?
jokes.setup: Jeff claimed to be sick to avoid helping with the move; Britta calls him suspicious
jokes.punchline: She narrows his possible locations to 'the Gap or Banana Republic' — two upscale-casual stores perfectly calibrated to Jeff's vanity and retail preferences
jokes.explanation: Smart character joke — the Gap/Banana Republic binary is both a burn on Jeff's specific vanity and a funny deductive leap. The specificity of those two stores does the heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Abed, we're moving the couch. This is historic.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: #CouchMovement2013

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, you're live-tweeting this?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Already got three retweets. This is trending in our apartment.

jokes.text: I'm pretending to be violently ill to avoid lifting a few boxes. Because I'm 13.
jokes.setup: Britta calls Jeff out for lying about being sick
jokes.punchline: Jeff sarcastically confesses in full, then adds 'Because I'm 13' — pre-emptively diminishing himself before Britta can
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-deprecating sarcasm is perfectly him — he'd rather mock himself than be sincerely caught. 'Because I'm 13' is punchy and quotable. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, I should have known it was a handicap space. There was a guy in a wheelchair yelling at me.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh sure, because wheelchair users are always yelling about parking spaces for their own personal gain.

jokes.text: And who's your primary care physician, Mr. Winger? Dr. Schroeder. S-C-H. Do you wanna see my insurance card? Please.
jokes.setup: Britta is interrogating Jeff about his fake illness; Jeff is playing along with mock sincerity
jokes.punchline: Jeff spells out the doctor's name and offers his insurance card — going full commitment to the bit, forcing Britta to say 'Please' and momentarily play into it
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the Jeff-lying bit — his commitment to the false alibi by volunteering a spelled-out name and insurance card is very Jeff. 'Please' from Britta is a funny concession. Solid, not brilliant.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You're not even sick! You just wanted to get out of studying. I can tell because you're wearing that expensive sweater from that store you said you'd never shop at again after they wouldn't give you a discount!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not true.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Then explain the tags still on it.

jokes.text: You hear that? That's not a heart monitor. It's a machine telling me I'm low on khakis.
jokes.setup: Britta hears what sounds like a hospital heart monitor beeping in the background of Jeff's call
jokes.punchline: Jeff reveals it's a retail inventory machine alerting him he's low on khakis — brilliantly confirming both that he's at the Gap AND satirizing his fashion-first priorities
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is elegant: Britta's suspicion about a beeping sound feels like a classic detective beat. The punchline — that the machine is tracking khaki stock levels — is a perfect comedic inversion that also reveals character. 'Low on khakis' as a medical emergency equivalent is a brilliant satirical reframe of Jeff's vanity. Economical, quotable, and deeply character-specific. Easily reaches the 8+ threshold.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're right, you caught me. I'm not actually sick. I'm faking it because I wanted to spend the day alone with you, but I knew you'd never go for that, so I had to fake appendicitis. It's all part of my master plan to slowly manipulate you into falling in love with me by appearing vulnerable and needy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: See? I knew it!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Also, I'm working with the Dean. We're trying to corner the market on fake illnesses so that when a real plague hits, people won't know who to trust.

jokes.text: Dr. Tarpenian to radiology, Dr. Tarpenian. [PA announcement plays in background while Jeff is at the Gap]
jokes.setup: Jeff has just claimed he's not at a hospital; a hospital PA plays in the background
jokes.punchline: The PA announcement immediately contradicts his denial, puncturing his lie in real time
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom irony — reality contradicts the character's claim immediately. Functional but not clever; we've seen this structure many times. The timing is good but the concept is well-worn.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, I'm at the hospital right now.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, you're not.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yes, I am. I got caught in some Gap machinery. My arm got tangled in a display of cardigans.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Jeff, that doesn't even make sense.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, it happened! I was trying on a medium when I should have grabbed a small, and the motion-activated rotating rack caught my sleeve. Now I'm in the emergency room with a fractured wrist and the doctor says I have to stop being so fashion-forward immediately.

jokes.text: You are fantastic. So are you. What are you doing after this? Probably trying a couple of boot-cuts. But after that, maybe, like, a blazer?
jokes.setup: Jeff has finessed his way through the fake illness cover story; a Gap employee compliments him
jokes.punchline: Jeff's post-crisis 'date' plan is trying on boot-cut jeans and maybe a blazer — revealing that this is genuinely his ideal Saturday
jokes.explanation: The joke confirms that Jeff's 'sick day' is genuinely how he wants to spend his Saturday — trying on clothes. The 'maybe, like, a blazer?' with uncertain inflection makes it funnier. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So what are you doing after the hospital?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I don't know, maybe go to the Gap?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: The Gap? What are you going to do there?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Try on some clothes.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, if you need any help with that, I'm available.

jokes.text: Nope, nothing in here. [Troy emerges from bathroom having clearly used all the tape]
jokes.setup: They've run out of packing tape; Troy went to check the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Troy emerges claiming there's nothing in there — but context (and presumably his appearance) makes clear he used ALL the tape in some elaborate way
jokes.explanation: Visual-dependent joke — the humor is in what Troy presumably looks like emerging from the bathroom having consumed all the tape. The transcript alone is thin, but the visual payoff (Troy wrapped in tape? tape covering something absurd?) would land well. Rewatch bonus for seeing the actual visual.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Well, you see, Annie, the tape is like a metaphorical bridge between the box and the void, and when you use all of it, you're essentially creating a temporal paradox that only exists in the space between Wednesday and Thursday.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's gold. I'm tweeting that.

jokes.text: You guys. You used all of it? I had a big breakfast.
jokes.setup: Annie is frustrated that all the packing tape has been used; she asks if they used it all
jokes.punchline: Abed says 'I had a big breakfast' — a completely non-sequitur explanation that implies the tape was consumed as food, which is insane, delivered with total deadpan sincerity
jokes.explanation: Exceptional absurdist joke. 'I had a big breakfast' as an explanation for consuming all the packing tape is perfectly Abed — the response implies a logical framework so bizarre it circles back to making complete sense in his world. The economy is perfect (five words), the character integration is total, and the deadpan delivery makes it funnier. This is exactly the kind of Abed joke that earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You know what? Men these days are just man-children. They never grow up.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Britta, you're really bad at comedy.

jokes.text: Nice. Tweeting it. [after the tape revelation]
jokes.setup: Abed has been live-tweeting the move all day
jokes.punchline: He announces he's tweeting the tape disaster — continuing to document everything regardless of content or relevance
jokes.explanation: Running gag execution — the tweeting bit returns to highlight Abed's compulsive documentation of all events regardless of their social media worthiness. Functional running gag, not elevated.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I can't live with them, I can't live without them.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Actually, you can live without us. We're not life support.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're more like... a really inconvenient habit.

jokes.text: There may be a slight danger I end up hating them. Man-children. Can't live with them, can't leave them alone with your tape.
jokes.setup: Annie, in a talking head, begins to admit her idealism may have been premature; starts riffing on the 'can't live with them' idiom
jokes.punchline: The punchline is '...can't leave them alone with your tape' — a hyper-specific, petty grievance subbing in for the expected 'can't live without them'
jokes.explanation: Smart play on the cliché — the substitution of 'your tape' for 'without them' is funny because it's simultaneously petty and entirely warranted. Annie's uptightness coming through as very precise grievance is good character writing.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: So there was this girl, right? And she went to Auschwitz...

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: ...and she did mushrooms.

jokes.text: Britta, don't make jokes. You're bad at it.
jokes.setup: Britta apparently makes a joke attempt in response to Annie's frustration
jokes.punchline: Annie flatly tells Britta she's bad at making jokes — a meta-commentary on Britta's well-established reputation in the group for being the unfunny one
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy and character-specific. 'Britta, don't make jokes. You're bad at it.' in Annie's matter-of-fact voice lands as both a character burn AND meta-acknowledgment of a show-wide running gag about Britta being annoying. The bluntness is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: So I met this guy at a party, and he was really into experimental drugs...

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is this one of your exes?

jokes.text: When I was in Amsterdam, I met this guy who ate too many shrooms, and fell out of a window at the Anne Frank House.
jokes.setup: Britta is trying to tell a comforting story to calm Annie down about the living situation
jokes.punchline: The ostensibly reassuring anecdote begins with someone eating too many shrooms and falling out of the Anne Frank House window — which is horrifying regardless of how it ends
jokes.explanation: Very Britta. The inappropriateness of the setting (Anne Frank House), the specificity (a friend of hers, in Amsterdam), and the casual way she deploys it as a pep talk is excellent character work. Dark but not gratuitous — the horror of the location makes the mundane drug story funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going to be more relaxed. Just go with the flow, you know? No more overthinking everything.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, did you say 'go with the flow' or 'go with the flow'? Because one has an implied acceptance of ambiguity, and the other is just... semantically lazy.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: And another thing—there should be a comma after 'you know,' not a question mark, because it's not actually interrogative, it's just a colloquialism, and—

jokes.text: Oh, no, no, he's fine. The doctor said that the drugs made his body just limp enough to keep him from breaking his neck.
jokes.setup: Britta is mid-anecdote about someone falling from the Anne Frank House
jokes.punchline: She clarifies he's fine — but the reason (drugs kept him limp enough) is itself disturbing and funny, the reassurance somehow making it worse
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous joke — 'the drugs made his body just limp enough' as the saving grace is a funny medical explanation that validates drug use as harm reduction in the most absurd way. Britta as an accidental advocate.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm totally chill. Like, fo' shizzle my nizzle.

jokes.text: Don't see what your taste in men has to do with my situation.
jokes.setup: Britta is using her Amsterdam story as a metaphor for Annie learning to 'go limp' with Troy and Abed
jokes.punchline: Annie misreads (or deliberately misreads) the story as being about Britta's romantic history, not a metaphor
jokes.explanation: Smart comic misdirection — Annie's reframe of the story as a romantic anecdote is a clever joke about how the Amsterdam story was told so poorly by Britta that it could easily be interpreted as a dating story. Tight and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We need to fix that outlet! It's a... a... outlet-y!

jokes.text: Shake it all up. Limp. Loosey-goosey. / Okay. New Annie. Going with the flow. / Is it loosey-goosey or goosey-loosey? Is it hyphenated? You know what? Don't tell me.
jokes.setup: Britta coaches Annie to relax and 'go limp, loosey-goosey'
jokes.punchline: Annie immediately fixates on the grammatical/lexical structure of 'loosey-goosey' — wondering if it's hyphenated — before catching herself and deciding not to know, as a form of willpower
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Annie attempting to relax by fixating on whether 'loosey-goosey' is hyphenated is a perfect expression of her compulsive need for correctness. The willpower in 'You know what? Don't tell me' — actively suppressing her instinct — is funny and deeply Annie. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I mean, how bad could it be? It's just drywall.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: #JustDrywallThings

jokes.text: You broke my pluggy thing. No worries. That's what the security deposit is for. Hashtag: That Is All.
jokes.setup: Someone throws a tape gun across the room, breaking something ('pluggy thing'); Annie starts to panic about the security deposit
jokes.punchline: Abed casually says that's what the security deposit is for, then signs off the live-tweet with 'Hashtag: That Is All' — a formal broadcast ending to what was a petty domestic incident
jokes.explanation: Running gag continues — 'Hashtag: That Is All' as a formal punctuation to a domestic disaster is a good Abed bit. The security deposit callback is also a minor setup for later (Pierce's subplot). Solid but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Don't worry, I'll fix it. I've been managing properties for years.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Back when I was a slumlord, we didn't have time for maintenance. Just collect the rent and move on.

jokes.text: I used to do that kind of thing when I was a slumlord.
jokes.setup: Pierce volunteers to fix the broken item before the landlord arrives; Annie is skeptical
jokes.punchline: Pierce casually mentions he used to handle this kind of thing 'when I was a slumlord' — revealing an entire horrible chapter of his past in one throwaway clause
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — 'when I was a slumlord' dropped into a helpful context is perfectly Pierce. His lack of shame about former exploitative landlordism, delivered as a mundane credential, is funny precisely because he doesn't see it as a confession. High character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: By 5 PM? Well, we're movin' on up, to the east side. To a deluxe apartment in the sky!

jokes.text: Easy peasy, George and Weezie.
jokes.setup: Pierce is reassuring Annie he can fix the broken item before the landlord arrives
jokes.punchline: 'Easy peasy, George and Weezie' — Pierce's racially-oblivious version of the idiom, substituting 'lemon squeezy' with a reference to The Jeffersons characters (a Black couple)
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Pierce joke. The substitution of 'lemon squeezy' with 'George and Weezie' (the Black Jeffersons characters) is a perfect expression of Pierce's specific brand of casual, clueless racism — he's not trying to be offensive, he's just pattern-matching in a way that reveals an embarrassing cultural framework. The joke earns its edge because it's entirely about character, not about punching down. One of the episode's highest-craft jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I'm worried about you all living together like this. You know what happened on Friends? They all ended up in complicated relationships, they had that whole thing with Ross and Rachel, and Monica had to organize everything!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: So what I'm saying is, one of you needs to be the Monica, one of you needs to be the Rachel, and somebody's gonna have to sleep with their brother.

jokes.text: I've seen enough Friends to know that cohabitation leads to sex, drugs, and something called Schwimmer-fatigue.
jokes.setup: Shirley expresses concern about Annie moving in with Troy and Abed
jokes.punchline: She grounds her concern in having watched Friends, warning of 'Schwimmer-fatigue' — a brilliantly specific, made-up condition named for David Schwimmer's character becoming grating
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. 'Schwimmer-fatigue' is an inspired coinage — it's funny as a warning about cohabitation (the Ross of the group eventually annoying everyone), it's funny as a media-literacy joke from Shirley who is using a TV show as a primary text for life advice, and it's quotable as a standalone concept. The structure builds perfectly from the legitimate-sounding 'sex, drugs' into the absurd 'Schwimmer-fatigue.' This earns its 8+ comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'll be the group's moral compass. Turns out I don't have one, so this should be fun.

jokes.text: Good, Shirley. What's the saying? If you can't stop them, judge them?
jokes.setup: Shirley says someone has to be the group's moral compass
jokes.punchline: Britta sarcastically rewrites 'If you can't beat them, join them' as 'If you can't stop them, judge them' — perfectly skewering Shirley's moralism
jokes.explanation: Very sharp cliché subversion. 'If you can't stop them, judge them' is a funny and accurate diagnosis of Shirley's actual strategy in life, and the rework of the idiom is clean and economical. High quotability — works as a standalone aphorism.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: This is just like that romantic movie where two people meet by chance and fall in love.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I haven't actually seen it though, because even I have standards.

jokes.text: Well, hey there, stranger. What a coincidence, huh? This is just like that Lake House movie. I can only assume. Even I have limits.
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton 'coincidentally' runs into Jeff at the mall on Saturday
jokes.punchline: He likens their encounter to The Lake House (a romantic film about two people destiny keeps bringing together), then admits he hasn't actually seen it — 'even I have limits'
jokes.explanation: Good Dean joke — his obsession with Jeff is played through the romantic movie reference, but the 'even I have limits' caveat is a nice self-aware beat that adds dimension. The Dean-stalking-Jeff dynamic is well-established and this executes it well.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: When I'm off campus, just call me Craig.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why would I do that?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Because that's my real name. I'm a Craigular guy.

jokes.text: Jeff, it's Saturday. Call me Craig. Off campus, I'm just a Craigular Joe.
jokes.setup: Jeff addresses the Dean formally; the Dean corrects him
jokes.punchline: 'Craigular Joe' — a pun on 'regular Joe' using his name Craig, delivered with complete earnestness as if it's a cool thing to say
jokes.explanation: 'Craigular Joe' is a genuinely good pun that works because the Dean delivers it like it's his cool-off-campus persona. The joke is enhanced by the Dean's complete sincerity — he thinks this is a good thing to call himself. High quotability, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Religious persecution? Britta, I'm not persecuting your religion. I'm persecuting YOU. There's a difference.

jokes.text: Curious. I might head there myself. I could tell them you said hi. / I'd rather you didn't. Well, maybe I won't have time. Especially if we're doing lunch?
jokes.setup: Dean mentions he could tell the study group Jeff is at the mall (not sick) instead of helping
jokes.punchline: He suggests the solution is 'doing lunch' — framing blackmail as a casual social invitation with plausible deniability
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean manipulation — dressing up coercion as a friendly social offer. The 'especially if we're doing lunch?' as the quid pro quo is funny in its casual framing of what is clearly extortion. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: No, it's because he's scary and we should definitely not help him.

jokes.text: Oh, look. A hitchhiker. A person in need. / Do not help him out. / Why, because it proves the existence of secular morality? / No, because he looks stinky.
jokes.setup: Shirley and Britta are arguing about whether atheism can produce morality; they spot a hitchhiker and Shirley sees him as a test case
jokes.punchline: Britta objects — but not on moral grounds; she says 'he looks stinky,' undercutting her atheist-morality position with shallow self-interest
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic reversal. Britta has been arguing for secular morality — but the moment she's tested, her objection to helping the hitchhiker is entirely aesthetic ('he looks stinky'). This is both a perfect Britta joke (her progressive ideals caving immediately to self-interest) and a smart philosophical comedy bit. Shirley's 'Judge not, Shirley. Judge not' follow-up adds another layer. High marks for structure and character.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my god, he's going all the way to Portland? That's like eight hours away!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: But you know what? I'm going to do it anyway because I'm an awesome person and I help people.

jokes.text: Where are you headed, fellow human?
jokes.setup: Shirley has picked up the hitchhiker and is being magnanimously charitable
jokes.punchline: 'Fellow human' — an oddly formal, slightly inhuman greeting that betrays how uncomfortable Shirley actually is with this stranger
jokes.explanation: 'Fellow human' is two words doing a lot of work — it signals that Shirley's charity is performative, she's uncomfortable, and she's defaulting to robotic formality when stressed. Good economy and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Hitchhiker
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for picking me up. God bless you.

dialogue.speaker: Hitchhiker
dialogue.line: Have you accepted Jesus Christ as your personal savior?

dialogue.speaker: Hitchhiker
dialogue.line: Because if you haven't, you're going to Hell, and I don't want that for you.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yeah, so... this is awkward.

jokes.text: Riverside Falls? That's 40 minutes away. Oh, I guess I'm just a really good person.
jokes.setup: The hitchhiker's destination is inconveniently far; Shirley has just committed to taking him
jokes.punchline: Shirley's self-congratulatory 'I guess I'm just a really good person' frames inconvenient charity as self-aggrandizement
jokes.explanation: Good Shirley beat — she's literally just inconvenienced herself and immediately spins it as evidence of her virtue. The self-satisfaction is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: If the room's a rockin', don't come a knockin'.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Actually, you should probably come knockin'. There's a gas leak.

jokes.text: I assume you both accepted Jesus Christ as your lord and savior? / Oh, that's nice.
jokes.setup: The hitchhiker has just been greeted warmly by Shirley (a devout Christian) and Britta (an atheist)
jokes.punchline: He immediately asks if they've accepted Jesus — a presumptuous question from a stranger — and Shirley, who would agree, responds with the deflecting 'Oh, that's nice' instead of enthusiastically affirming, because the context makes her uncomfortable
jokes.explanation: Setup for the larger Jesus reveal. Shirley's 'Oh, that's nice' is a good deflection — she's been put in an ironic position where a stranger's religiosity makes her uncomfortable. Solid but functions mainly as a bridge joke.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, is this really a two-bedroom apartment?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Your room is blankets.

jokes.text: Needed a coat of paint anyway. [Pierce has apparently destroyed something in Annie's old apartment while trying to fix it]
jokes.setup: Pierce was supposed to fix the 'pluggy thing' before Annie's landlord arrives
jokes.punchline: The damage is severe enough that it needs 'a coat of paint' — Pierce's minimizing spin on obvious destruction
jokes.explanation: Good visual-implied joke. Pierce's 'needed a coat of paint anyway' as a minimizing spin on clearly catastrophic home repair damage is classic Pierce obliviousness. The understatement does the work.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: A blanket fort isn't just a place, it's a lifestyle. It's a philosophy. You're not running from the world, you're creating your own world where the only rule is comfort. And in that world, everything from birthday parties to funerals happens naturally. Death? That's just another blanket fort occasion.

jokes.text: What's your name, friend? Jesus. / Are you Latino? / No, my child. I am him. / You're what now? I am the one true son of God. I was sent here to save humanity.
jokes.setup: The hitchhiker has been riding along; Shirley asks his name
jokes.punchline: His name is Jesus — but then he clarifies he's not Latino, he IS Jesus Christ. The reveal escalates from a name coincidence to genuine messianic delusion
jokes.explanation: The 'Are you Latino?' from Shirley is a perfect beat — it's her attempting to find a mundane explanation before having to confront the actual claim. The escalation from name → Latino assumption → actual Jesus claim is well-structured. The situation mines the Shirley/Britta dynamic (Christian vs. atheist) perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, you guys haven't built a blanket fort yet? I thought that's what you'd do first!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Actually, we have plans. We're gonna use your bedroom as our TV room.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're calling it 'Fort Blanket.'

jokes.text: So inspiring how he came to find the lord. Isn't it, Britta? Yeah, yeah. Well, I didn't exactly have to find the lord. He was inside me. Amen.
jokes.setup: Shirley praises how the hitchhiker 'found the lord,' framing his story in Christian terms
jokes.punchline: The hitchhiker corrects her — he didn't find the lord, 'He was inside me' — meaning he is Jesus, which Shirley accepts with 'Amen' without registering what he said
jokes.explanation: Good layered joke — the hitchhiker's correction ('He was inside me') is a theologically specific statement that Shirley misreads as humility before he reveals he literally means he is Jesus. Shirley's 'Amen' is the perfect non-reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: What's a linen closet?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what would you like to order?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I don't know, what do you have?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: Well, we have our specials today...

jokes.text: Hey Jesus, just curious, what's your position on marijuana? / It was given to us by God. It should be legal. / Oh, that's nice.
jokes.setup: The hitchhiker has claimed to be Jesus; Britta sees an opportunity to co-opt him for her politics
jokes.punchline: Jesus endorses marijuana legalization; Shirley's disapproval lands as 'Oh, that's nice' — a callback to her earlier nervous deflection, now reversed (this time SHE's the uncomfortable one)
jokes.explanation: Smart callback structure — Shirley's 'Oh, that's nice' returns, but this time she's the one being theologically destabilized. Britta immediately polling Jesus on marijuana policy is perfect Britta. The reversal of positions (Britta delighted, Shirley dismayed) makes this a high-craft moment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's blackmail.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: It's not blackmail, it's... leverage.

jokes.text: Presenting the real-life fairy tale of how princess Annie was saved from Bad Neighborhood Forest by Woodsman Troy. And Bebad, his emotionally unavailable unicorn.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed introduce a puppet/blanket-fort fairy tale for Annie on her moving day
jokes.punchline: Abed is 'Bebad, his emotionally unavailable unicorn' — a self-aware character description that acknowledges Abed's known emotional affect while casting himself as a magical creature
jokes.explanation: 'Emotionally unavailable unicorn' is a perfect character joke. It's both a self-aware gag about Abed's emotional detachment AND a funny fairy-tale framing (unicorns being magical but aloof). The name 'Bebad' (a playful compression of 'Abed') is a cute touch. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Well, that's... that's wonderful. I mean, I'm happy for you, I really am. But you understand why I might be a little skeptical, right? I mean, no offense, but you look more like you need a shower than you need followers.

jokes.text: Brought to you by the girl-yogurt Jamie Lee Curtis uses to poo. A package of it is in the fridge.
jokes.setup: Abed is narrating the fairy tale in a formal voice
jokes.punchline: He adds a commercial sponsor tag in the middle of the fairy tale — specifically Jamie Lee Curtis's Activia yogurt (then-famous for its ads about digestive regularity) — and notes there's some in the fridge
jokes.explanation: Brilliant meta joke. The commercial break interruption of the fairy tale is funny; the specific choice of Activia yogurt ('the girl-yogurt Jamie Lee Curtis uses to poo') is funnier; the kicker 'A package of it is in the fridge' — grounding the absurd ad in domestic reality — is the perfect button. The logic that they have this yogurt in the fridge and chose to work it into the fairy tale sponsor slot is impeccable.

dialogue.speaker: Jesus
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Jesus Christ.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Jesus
dialogue.line: Actually, that's my dad.

jokes.text: Oh, come on, Jeffrey. Get in here. This is gonna be fun. Or else.
jokes.setup: Dean is forcing Jeff to participate in a karaoke/singing activity at the mall
jokes.punchline: 'This is gonna be fun. Or else.' — the Dean's threat is delivered with cheerful menace, the 'or else' making explicit that this fun is mandatory
jokes.explanation: Very economical — 'This is gonna be fun. Or else.' captures the entire Dean-blackmail dynamic in five words. The juxtaposition of forced cheerfulness with implicit threat is a good bit of character compression.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: So Jesus, what's your stance on marijuana legalization?

dialogue.speaker: Jesus
dialogue.line: I'm totally cool with it. In fact, I think all drugs should be legal.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: See? I knew you'd say that.

jokes.text: Unless you wanna be back here next Saturday. / Okay, you know this one, Jeff. We've sang it a thousand times together in my mind.
jokes.setup: Dean is pressuring Jeff to sing karaoke with him; Jeff is resistant
jokes.punchline: 'We've sang it a thousand times together in my mind' — the Dean reveals he has an elaborate fantasy life involving Jeff that includes karaoke duets
jokes.explanation: One of the Dean's best lines. 'We've sang it a thousand times together in my mind' is simultaneously deeply unsettling and deeply funny — it reveals the Dean's fantasy life while maintaining his oblivious sincerity about sharing this with Jeff directly to his face. This is exactly the kind of line that makes the Dean character iconic. High marks across the board.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And in this fairy tale, Abed is an emotionally unavailable unicorn.

jokes.text: ♪ Jesus loves marijuana ♪ / ♪ And drinking human blood ♪
jokes.setup: Everyone in the car has been singing along to 'Kiss From a Rose'; the hitchhiker Jesus starts adding his own verses
jokes.punchline: Jesus inserts 'Jesus loves marijuana' and then 'and drinking human blood' as lyrics — the second line a dark twist that pivots from marijuana advocacy to communion cannibalism
jokes.explanation: The escalation from weed endorsement to 'drinking human blood' is a perfect dark turn — especially because the blood reference is theologically accurate (communion) which makes it MORE disturbing that he's singing it in a car. The juxtaposition with the earnest Seal song is inspired.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know what Activia commercials are? They're just women talking about their digestive systems. That's it. That's the whole commercial. A woman goes, 'I couldn't go to the bathroom, but then I ate this yogurt and now I'm pooping regularly.' Congratulations on your regular bowel movements, Karen. Want a medal?

jokes.text: Ha, ha. Ah! That was great. Yeah, might have been a little fun.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Dean have just finished a karaoke duet; Jeff has been forced into it
jokes.punchline: Jeff admits 'might have been a little fun' — a reluctant concession that the Dean's blackmail forced Jeff into something he actually enjoyed, which is mortifying for Jeff
jokes.explanation: The humor is in Jeff's pride cracking — his understatement ('might have been a little fun') is very Jeff. It also sets up his further humiliation when the Dean reveals the email. Character-consistent, moderately funny.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Wait, who is that singing with us?

dialogue.speaker: Jesus
dialogue.line: I'm Jesus. I just wanted to join in on the communion song.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That's... that's not what communion is about.

dialogue.speaker: Jesus
dialogue.line: No? Because I've been telling people to take this body, take this blood, turn it into whatever they want...

jokes.text: And you e-mailed your therapist that you wanted to be alone this weekend. What?
jokes.setup: Jeff is warming to his forced outing with the Dean; the Dean drops another piece of information he shouldn't have
jokes.punchline: The Dean reveals he's read Jeff's private emails, including one to his therapist about wanting to be alone — making the forced social outing even more psychologically pointed
jokes.explanation: Good Dean escalation — revealing he's been reading Jeff's therapy emails adds a genuinely unsettling layer to his obsession. The pivot from 'this was fun' to 'you're surveilling me' is a good tonal shift.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I read your private emails to your therapist.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: What? Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Because I care about you, Jeffrey. And frankly, some of your sessions are hilarious.

jokes.text: And now, with your permission, I'd like to sing a little song about race-mixing. This one's called 'Don't You Do It.' Get out! Get out!
jokes.setup: Jesus has been a charming/absurd guest who endorsed marijuana and sang Seal; the car has been going along with him
jokes.punchline: He announces a song about 'race-mixing' — the reveal that the messianic vagrant was going to pivot to racism finally snaps both Shirley and Britta into unified agreement to eject him
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the Jesus subplot — after all the theological chaos, it takes a song about 'race-mixing' to get Shirley and Britta to agree on something. The structure is elegant: the entire bit has been escalating toward the moment that unifies two opposites. The title 'Don't You Do It' is a funny pseudo-protest song title.

dialogue.speaker: Jesus
dialogue.line: I could sing a song about race-mixing.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Now the Patriot Act says I can do it, Jeffrey, technically. Need I remind you the nation is at war?
jokes.setup: Jeff confronts the Dean for reading his private school emails; the Dean defends himself
jokes.punchline: He invokes the Patriot Act and national security as justification for reading his student's emails to a therapist — a reductio ad absurdum of surveillance law applied to mundane institutional nosiness
jokes.explanation: 'Need I remind you the nation is at war?' applied to reading a community college student's therapy emails is a perfect absurdist escalation of institutional overreach. The Dean's earnest delivery of this justification makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Dean, you can't just read students' emails.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Jeff, in a post-9/11 world, I have to consider every email a potential threat. Last week, Shirley wrote 'I'm bringing brownies to the study group.' Brownies? That could be code.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: That's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Is it? Or is it *necessary*?

jokes.text: I'll kill you. No, Jeffrey, no. Jeffrey, come on. / Don't let the terrorists win!
jokes.setup: Jeff threatens the Dean physically; the Dean de-escalates with increasingly absurd appeals
jokes.punchline: 'Don't let the terrorists win!' — the Dean repurposes 9/11-era patriotic rhetoric as self-defense against Jeff strangling him
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Patriot Act bit — the Dean weaponizes 'don't let the terrorists win' as literal self-preservation from Jeff's anger. The escalation from surveillance law to physical altercation defused by anti-terrorism rhetoric is a great compressed bit. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You invaded my privacy! You went through my files!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, if you're going to get this angry about it, then the terrorists have already won.

jokes.text: And then the three of them lived happily ever after. Yay! Bebad became the little dipper. The end. Kiss me, Woodsman Troy. Muah.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are wrapping up their fairy-tale presentation for Annie
jokes.punchline: 'Bebad became the little dipper' as an ending — a random, cosmically absurd fate for the character, plus Annie asking Troy to kiss her as the princess kissing the woodsman
jokes.explanation: 'Bebad became the little dipper' is a perfectly random fairy-tale ending — constellations as a fate is a classic folk-tale ending that works here as an absurdist riff. Annie asking Troy to kiss her is sweet and funny in context. Solid closing beat to the fairy tale sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And this is the second bedroom. Or as I like to call it, my imagination playroom.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Your imagination playroom?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's a safe space for adults to explore their inner child without judgment or responsibility.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Abed, there's nothing in here.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Exactly. The possibilities are infinite.

jokes.text: Let's make the entire apartment a fort. I'll get more blankets.
jokes.setup: Annie has been won over by the fairy tale; she's now fully buying into Troy and Abed's world
jokes.punchline: She immediately escalates to wanting to fort the entire apartment — the most extreme version of going with the flow
jokes.explanation: Sweet character moment — Annie's conversion from uptight to fort-enthusiast in one fairy tale is funny. The escalation from 'accepting the blanket fort' to 'fort THE WHOLE APARTMENT' is good but not surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I am so tired of jumping through hoops around here!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, there are literally hoops in the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I know! That's what I'm talking about!

jokes.text: This is a space we reserved for virtual adventures. Like a playroom, but only works in our minds. We call it the Dreamatorium. / But it's a bedroom.
jokes.setup: Annie discovers there IS a second bedroom that could have been her room
jokes.punchline: Troy and Abed have converted it to the 'Dreamatorium' — a room that only 'works in their minds' — a room whose entire value is imaginary, while Annie sleeps in a blanket fort
jokes.explanation: Great payoff — the Dreamatorium reveal is both the episode's major structural joke (an entire bedroom reserved for imagination while Annie sleeps in a fort) and a defining statement of Troy and Abed's character. 'Like a playroom, but only works in our minds' is a perfect, economical description of absurd childlike logic. Annie's flat 'But it's a bedroom' is the perfect straight-man response.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You have to choose. It's either me or the dreamatorium.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Well, actually, according to Lease Amendment 7, subsection C, written in crayon and signed by both of us, the dreamatorium is a protected space.

jokes.text: Dreamatorium is non-negotiable. Read the lease. The part added in crayon. Don't wanna take this to court. Could be a court in the blink of an eye.
jokes.setup: Annie demands either the Dreamatorium becomes a bedroom or she's leaving
jokes.punchline: Troy and Abed invoke the lease — specifically the part written in crayon — and threaten to turn the room into a court 'in the blink of an eye' (imagining it, presumably)
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest beats. 'Read the lease. The part added in crayon.' is an instant classic — the casual invocation of a crayon amendment as a legally binding document. The threat to turn the room into a court 'in the blink of an eye' (via imagination) is a perfect expression of their power in this space. Very quotable, high craft.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We could film it in the Dreamatorium. It's versatile. We did a whole courtroom drama in there last week.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You did?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No, but we could.

jokes.text: Me or this stupid Dreamatorium. / Dreamatorium is non-negotiable. Read the lease. / The part added in crayon.
jokes.setup: Annie delivers an ultimatum about the Dreamatorium
jokes.punchline: Troy's addition: 'The part added in crayon' — confirming that there is a crayon addendum to a legally binding lease document, written and apparently enforced
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. 'Read the lease — the part added in crayon' is a perfect joke. It implies: (a) they actually added to their lease, (b) in crayon, (c) presumably including the word 'Dreamatorium,' and (d) they expect this to hold up. The specificity of 'crayon' — not marker, not pen, crayon — is the right choice. Only Troy and Abed. Very high quotability and rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: There, there. Want me to read you a bedtime story?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Pierce, I'm 19 years old. I don't need a bedtime story.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. Want to play with my trains?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No! I want Annie to come back!

jokes.text: I picked the wrong week to quit. [Pierce takes a candy cigarette]
jokes.setup: Annie has stormed out; Troy and Abed are sad; Pierce offers candy cigarettes and says he doesn't want candy
jokes.punchline: 'I picked the wrong week to quit' — a parody of the classic movie cliché ('I picked the wrong week to quit drinking/sniffing glue' from Airplane!) but applied to candy cigarettes, which deflates the drama
jokes.explanation: Classic Community pop-culture reference — the Airplane! callback works because it undercuts the dramatic moment with a cliché about candy. The deflation from dramatic to candy is good. Not the sharpest pop-culture joke the show has done but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I was walking through the parking lot, and these island girls came up to me. They said they wanted to show me their culture. Next thing I know, I'm waking up in a dumpster behind the Food Court with a concussion and what I'm pretty sure is a tattoo of a mai tai on my shoulder.

jokes.text: What the hell is this? In security deposit terms, it's a gold mine.
jokes.setup: Annie returns to her old apartment to find Pierce's 'repair' has made things far worse (structural damage, etc.)
jokes.punchline: Pierce reframes the disaster as a 'gold mine' in security deposit terms — meaning he's apparently so versed in slumlord economics that he sees catastrophic damage as an opportunity
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Pierce's slumlord history — 'in security deposit terms, it's a gold mine' reframes catastrophe through his exploitative landlord lens. Character-specific and pays off the earlier setup.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: How long was I out?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Three days.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Three days? That's like... 21 Matlock episodes!

jokes.text: I had some island girls over and one of them must have slipped me a mickey.
jokes.setup: Pierce explains why he destroyed Annie's apartment
jokes.punchline: His explanation — that 'island girls' slipped him a mickey — is a comically implausible excuse that tells us more about Pierce's delusions of desirability than it explains anything
jokes.explanation: Very Pierce — the 'island girls' detail is doing a lot of work in revealing his self-image. The implausibility functions as the joke. Not the sharpest but character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, back in my day, we shared files the old-fashioned way.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: We used Napster.

jokes.text: Is Napster still a thing?
jokes.setup: Annie explains Pierce has been unconscious long enough for her to realize she needs to keep living alone
jokes.punchline: Pierce's first question upon hearing this is whether Napster still exists — a perfect revelation that he was unconscious long enough to wonder about early-2000s file sharing services, and also just very Pierce
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — three words that do enormous work. 'Is Napster still a thing?' establishes that Pierce has been out long enough to wonder about his cultural reference points, AND it's a perfect Pierce cultural touchstone (he'd be using Napster). The single question is funnier than any explanation could be. High marks for economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: My shoulder's been killing me. I can't be held responsible for anything I say or do.

jokes.text: You've been out long enough for me to realize I'm gonna need to keep living alone. Is Napster still a thing?
jokes.setup: Annie tells Pierce how long he's been unconscious
jokes.punchline: Pierce asks if Napster is still a thing — a reference so dated that it immediately signals both how out of touch he is AND how long he might have been unconscious (Napster died circa 2001)
jokes.explanation: Good Pierce temporal disorientation joke. 'Is Napster still a thing?' establishes how profoundly out of touch Pierce is — Napster shut down in 2001, so either he's very confused or very groggy. Works as a quick, economical Pierce character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm sorry for my behavior. I know I can be difficult sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's just that my mind works differently. Like, imagine a TV show, but the laugh track is playing at random intervals, and all the characters are actors within actors, and there's a meta-commentary running on a ticker at the bottom of the screen constantly analyzing whether the meta-commentary itself is meta enough.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Plus, there are three separate timelines playing simultaneously, but only I can see them, and one of them is a stop-motion animation, and another is shot in the style of a Wong Kar-wai film, but everything's also somehow a reference to something that hasn't been made yet, and my thoughts come with DVD commentary that I can't turn off.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So yeah. That's just how it is up here.

jokes.text: Oh, what the hell? I have brain damage. Nothing I do counts.
jokes.setup: Pierce is apparently doing something inappropriate or destructive; Annie protests
jokes.punchline: Pierce invokes 'brain damage' as a blanket moral exemption — 'nothing I do counts' — a horrifying logical leap delivered with gleeful relief
jokes.explanation: Pierce at his darkly comic best. 'I have brain damage. Nothing I do counts.' is both a character-specific dodge AND a genuinely funny philosophical claim. The delight in his delivery (he's clearly going to exploit this exemption) is exactly right. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going to be more laid-back about the room. Whatever works for you guys.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: But these pillows need to be arranged by thread count, and they should be fluffed in a counter-clockwise motion.

jokes.text: Oh, what the hell? I have brain damage. Nothing I do counts.
jokes.setup: Pierce is recovering from whatever happened; Annie tells him to come help clean up
jokes.punchline: Pierce claims brain damage as blanket absolution for his behavior — 'nothing I do counts' — a flawless Pierce logic of weaponizing victimhood
jokes.explanation: 'I have brain damage. Nothing I do counts.' is a perfect Pierce sentence. It's a logical syllogism with no actual logical validity — brain damage doesn't create moral immunity — but Pierce delivers it with such confidence that it almost holds. The two sentences work together perfectly. Highly quotable, strongly character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie, can you help me with something? I need to iron my shirt.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Of course! Do you know how to use an iron?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, I got this. You just... turn it on and... wait, which end do I use?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Troy, the flat part. The flat part goes on the shirt.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh. So you don't, like, rub it like a magic lamp?

jokes.text: Where does water go in the iron? / What's the iron for? / What gets out Kool-Aid stains? / The opposite color Kool-Aid doesn't work.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed have revealed they've redecorated for Annie; now they reveal the domestic helplessness behind their invitation
jokes.punchline: Their actual needs: they don't know how an iron works, what an iron is for, how to remove Kool-Aid stains (apparently tried matching-color Kool-Aid), and Troy has an infected wound from fork jousting
jokes.explanation: Great escalating list of their actual domestic incompetence. 'The opposite color Kool-Aid doesn't work' is a perfect revelation — it implies they tried it, which is insane. 'Fork jousting' as a household activity is excellent. Each item is funnier than the last.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: How do you get Kool-aid stains out?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You use more Kool-aid. It cancels out.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not how stains work.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude.

jokes.text: But what about the Dreamatorium? It's more important than us. You're more important than our room.
jokes.setup: Annie asks about the Dreamatorium's fate; Troy answers earnestly
jokes.punchline: 'It's more important than us' — Annie's sarcastic reading of their earlier position — is then sincerely denied by Troy, who insists Annie outranks a room
jokes.explanation: Decent emotional beat more than a joke. The resolution of the Dreamatorium conflict has mild comedy in Troy's earnest prioritization, but it's doing emotional work here rather than comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Jeff, I noticed you have exactly seventeen pictures of yourself on your mantle. That's not vanity—that's a cry for help. Also, your apartment smells like cologne and broken dreams.

jokes.text: This is all gay code.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are being sweet and sincere about Annie being more important than their room
jokes.punchline: Pierce, apparently present, flatly declares 'This is all gay code' — his reflexive interpretation of any male emotional expression
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce obliviousness joke — his go-to interpretation of male emotional vulnerability as 'gay code' is consistent characterization, though the type of joke is well-worn for Pierce. Economy is excellent (three words), but the originality is limited.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We've been playing a lot of paintball lately.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I think I have a concussion.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's just your brain getting better at paintball.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not how concussions work.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude.

jokes.text: Troy scraped me when we were fork-jousting last week. I don't think it's healing. / Oh! That's infected.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed have been listing domestic problems they need Annie's help with
jokes.punchline: 'Fork-jousting' — a sport apparently practiced regularly in their apartment — has left Abed with an infected wound
jokes.explanation: 'Fork-jousting' is a perfect made-up activity for Troy and Abed — sounds exactly like something they'd do with complete seriousness. The casualness of 'I don't think it's healing' and Annie's immediate diagnosis ('That's infected') is a good comedic beat about their need for adult supervision.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Okay Troy, we're now entering the Gamma Quadrant. Jeff, you're Horsebot 3000.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, why is Jeff a horse?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Because he's majestic and vain.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not doing this.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Come on Jeff, just go with it!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Horsebot 3000, we need you to calculate our trajectory using your equine instincts.

jokes.text: Infected. That's the word.
jokes.setup: Annie diagnoses Abed's wound as infected
jokes.punchline: Abed's response is 'That's the word' — implying he knew something was wrong but lacked vocabulary, delivered with his characteristic clinical affect
jokes.explanation: 'That's the word.' is perfect Abed deadpan — maximum economy, completely in character. It implies he was describing it to himself differently, which raises more questions. Beautifully understated.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, I found his weak spot!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It's his... belly button. He's extremely ticklish.

jokes.text: Hi, guys. I thought you were sick. / I wasn't. I kind of made it up to get out of helping. / Oh, that's okay. / It is? Yeah, it is.
jokes.setup: Jeff arrives at the apartment after his day with the Dean; he confesses to faking his illness
jokes.punchline: The group immediately forgives him — 'Oh, that's okay / It is? Yeah, it is.' — revealing that his elaborate lie was completely unnecessary, which makes his entire subplot feel worse
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff — Jeff's punishment for avoiding the move was spending the day with the Dean, only to find out no one cared anyway. The 'Oh, that's okay / It is? Yeah, it is.' exchange is a good tag on the episode's moral: Jeff's self-serving behavior hurt only himself.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I actually had fun.

jokes.text: Oh, hey, Jeff, did you know that when it snows my eyes become large? ♪ And the light that you shine can be seen ♪ / He tweeted it? He tweeted it!
jokes.setup: Jeff has just confessed his lie; the Dean arrives and says something bizarre about his eyes in snow
jokes.punchline: The Dean has apparently tweeted (via Abed's Annie's Move hashtag?) about his day with Jeff; the reveal is captured in Abed's horrified 'He tweeted it?' — meaning Jeff's humiliating day is now public record
jokes.explanation: Smart convergence of two running threads — the live-tweeting gag and Jeff's Dean subplot collide in the reveal that the Dean tweeted something (likely the karaoke, the hand-holding, all of it). 'Did you know that when it snows my eyes become large?' is also a sublimely weird Dean non sequitur that lands perfectly.

jokes.text: He tweeted it? He tweeted it! [Abed has apparently live-tweeted Jeff's admission that he faked sick]
jokes.setup: Jeff confesses he faked being sick; Abed is live-tweeting everything
jokes.punchline: Jeff realizes in real time that Abed has just tweeted his confession to the world
jokes.explanation: Solid running gag payoff. The live-tweet gag has been building all episode and this is its final punchline — Jeff's lie is now public record. The repeated 'He tweeted it?' / 'He tweeted it!' structure captures Jeff's disbelief escalating to horror.

jokes.text: Thanks for getting us to planet Greendalia safely, Horse-bot 3000. Oh, no. Greendalia has been overrun by evil King Blorgon.
jokes.setup: Post-reconciliation, the apartment is fully in Dreamatorium mode; Annie has joined their game
jokes.punchline: They're playing an elaborate space opera; Annie has become Horse-bot 3000; Abed introduces 'King Blorgon' as the villain — specific, silly names delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the episode's theme — Annie has fully integrated into Troy and Abed's world. 'King Blorgon' and 'Horse-bot 3000' are funny names delivered with the earnestness that makes Troy and Abed great. The resolution-through-absurdity is very Community.

jokes.text: Oh, no. Greendalia has been overrun by evil King Blorgon. Look out, Troyborg. Ahh! I'm dead. Horse-bot 3000, no. I love you.
jokes.setup: The Dreamatorium space adventure takes a turn — an evil king attacks
jokes.punchline: Troy dies immediately ('I'm dead'), then has a death scene declaring love for Horse-bot 3000 — a fully committed performance of a ridiculous narrative
jokes.explanation: Troy's instant death and deathbed love confession to Horse-bot 3000 is played with total commitment. The name 'Troyborg' and 'King Blorgon' both demonstrate the specific absurdist naming register of their universe, and Troy's earnest 'I love you' to a robot horse is a great character beat.

jokes.text: Aim for his butt. It's his only weakness.
jokes.setup: In their space opera game, they're fighting King Blorgon whose 'lasers are useless against me'
jokes.punchline: Abed identifies the butt as King Blorgon's only weakness — delivered with the gravity of a tactical insight
jokes.explanation: Classic absurdist game-logic — 'aim for his butt' as a tactical revelation is funny in its specificity and earnestness. The delivery ('it's his only weakness') frames the butt as a solemn strategic fact. Simple but effective.

jokes.text: Aim for his butt. It's his only weakness.
jokes.setup: King Blorgon declares their lasers are useless against him
jokes.punchline: Abed instructs to aim for his butt — his only weakness — a tactical detail delivered with the same gravity as a real battle strategy
jokes.explanation: 'Aim for his butt. It's his only weakness.' — delivered with complete tactical sincerity — is a gem. The specificity of the butt as the singular weakness of an evil alien king, stated as established fact, is excellent absurdist economy. 'It's his only weakness' as the confirmatory second sentence is what elevates it from a cheap joke to a great one.

jokes.text: Five minutes and we should probably put a stop to this. / Jeff, are you... / I liked Horse-bot 3000.
jokes.setup: Jeff has apparently been drawn into the Dreamatorium game despite himself; Annie checks on him
jokes.punchline: 'I liked Horse-bot 3000.' — Jeff quietly confesses attachment to the imaginary robot horse he played, in the same tone he admitted the Dean's day was 'a little fun'
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing character beat. 'I liked Horse-bot 3000.' is four words that complete Jeff's arc — the man who faked illness to avoid his friends has been won over by an imaginary robot horse. The quiet sincerity mirrors his earlier 'might have been a little fun' and both undercut his cool-guy persona. Economical, character-perfect, and emotionally resonant. Strong closer.

tmdb_overview: Annie has second thoughts about moving in with Troy and Abed once she realizes that they expect her to live in a blanket fort.
insight: Character comedy carries 77-point episode through absurdist dance-floor chaos with steady three jokes per minute.
